passage:
Tenzin, sit with your Ganga aunty a minute. You remind me of myself at twenty-five, watching someone the way you're watching Sonam now. Mine was Prakash, at the tea company office in Siliguri. He took every late shift, ate lunch over spreadsheets, stopped coming to our Saturday badminton. He got promoted twice in a year.
I'll be honest, first I was jealous. Then one evening I saw him fall asleep sitting up at his desk, pen still in his hand, and the jealousy just went.
I didn't lecture him about balance. I said, 'I'm getting momos at seven. Come for twenty minutes, then go back to your work.' He came. He laughed for the first time in weeks.
He still wanted the promotion, and he got it. But he came every Thursday after that.

qa.q: What did Prakash stop coming to?
qa.a: Our Saturday badminton, as Ganga puts it.

qa.q: What made Ganga's jealousy of Prakash turn into concern?
qa.a: Seeing him fall asleep sitting up at his desk, pen still in his hand, showed how worn out he was, and the jealousy went.

qa.q: What choice did Ganga make instead of lecturing Prakash, and why did it work?
qa.a: She invited him for momos for twenty minutes and told him to go back to his work after, offering a break without questioning his goals.

qa.q: What might Prakash have felt when invited for just twenty minutes?
qa.a: Prakash may have felt relieved and cared for, since the invitation respected his work instead of criticising it.

grounding: Shows a colleague who sees a peer giving up sleep and friendships for promotion, moves from envy to concern, and offers a break without judging his goals.

passage:
Rain had flooded the lane outside the insurance office, and half the staff had gone home early. Deepak hadn't. Minakshi found him at eight, still at his desk, eyes red, three empty tea cups lined up by the keyboard. He had skipped his cousin's engagement last Sunday to finish the quarterly report, and he'd missed every team lunch since March.
Minakshi felt a twist of envy first. The regional head praised him in every meeting. Then she noticed his hand shaking as he reached for a fourth cup.
She sat on the edge of the next desk. 'I'm not telling you to stop going for team lead. You'd be good. But the water's rising and the last bus leaves at nine. I'll take the claims file tomorrow morning. Go home and sleep tonight?'
He looked at the window, then at her, and slowly saved his work.

qa.q: What did Deepak skip last Sunday to finish the quarterly report?
qa.a: His cousin's engagement.

qa.q: What did Minakshi feel first, and what changed it?
qa.a: She felt a twist of envy because the regional head praised him, then concern when she noticed his hand shaking as he reached for more tea.

qa.q: Which choice by Minakshi made the offer easy for Deepak to accept?
qa.a: She said she wasn't asking him to stop going for team lead and offered to take the claims file, so the break didn't question his goal.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel hearing 'You'd be good' from a colleague?
qa.a: He might feel seen and less defensive, since his ambition was respected rather than judged.

grounding: Shows a colleague watching a peer sacrifice sleep and relationships for promotion, setting aside envy and offering a break out of genuine concern.

passage: By the third month, Asif had stopped counting how many nights Aparna stayed past midnight in their Lower Parel office. She had skipped her college reunion, stopped going to her dance class, and lived on vending-machine chips. Some colleagues whispered that she was sucking up for the promotion. Asif felt a twinge of envy himself; the director had praised her twice already. But mostly he noticed the dark circles, and how her hand shook holding her coffee. On Friday he stopped by her desk with two cups of cutting chai. "I'm not saying slow down. You're going to get that promotion. I'm just saying, come for a twenty-minute walk. The report will still be here." She stared at him. Then she stood up.

qa.q: What did Asif bring to Aparna's desk?
qa.a: Two cups of cutting chai.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Asif have watching Aparna?
qa.a: He felt a twinge of envy at her praise, but mostly concern at her dark circles and shaking hand.

qa.q: Why did Asif's approach work better than the whispers?
qa.a: He showed genuine concern without judging her goal, offering a short break instead of criticism.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel when Asif says she'll get the promotion?
qa.a: Aparna may feel surprised and relieved to be supported rather than judged.

grounding: Shows a colleague who notices someone sacrificing sleep and health for promotion, and offers a break out of concern rather than envy.

passage:
"Payal, it's nine. You were here at seven this morning."
"The regional head reviews the numbers tomorrow, Vikas. If I nail this, the manager post is mine."
"You'll nail it. You always do." Vikas put a box of idlis on her desk. "When did you last eat something that wasn't biscuits?"
"Don't lecture me."
"I'm not. Honestly, I'm a bit jealous of how good you are at this."
She laughed, surprised.
"But you missed your sister's engagement. And you've had that cough for three weeks."
Payal looked at the idlis. "I'll sleep after the promotion."
"That's what you said after the last one." He sat on the edge of the next desk. "Eat. Ten minutes. Then I'll leave you to it. I just miss the Payal who came to Friday cricket."
She picked up an idli.

qa.q: What did Vikas put on Payal's desk?
qa.a: A box of idlis.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling as he talked to Payal?
qa.a: He felt worried about her health and admitted being a bit jealous, but his care was stronger.

qa.q: What did Vikas do well that others could copy?
qa.a: He named his envy honestly, backed her goal and asked only for a ten-minute break.

qa.q: What is it like for Payal to hear she was missed at Friday cricket?
qa.a: Payal may feel touched and a little sad, realising what she has given up.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague expressing concern, not judgement or envy, for a peer sacrificing health and relationships for promotion.

passage:
Buddy-mentor note, month four. Hrithik, the most driven analyst on our floor, slept at his desk again on Tuesday; the cleaner found him at six. He has quit his cricket league, skipped two family weddings and missed his own birthday lunch to finish the pricing model. I'll be honest: part of me envies how fast he's rising. But at lunch today his hands were shaking, and he couldn't remember what he'd eaten. I didn't tell him he was wrong to want the promotion. I said, "I want you to get it. I also want you around after you do." He laughed it off, then asked if the Saturday morning walk I'd mentioned was still on. Next step: I'll meet him at the park gate at seven on Saturday.
Parveen

qa.q: Who found Hrithik asleep at his desk?
qa.a: The cleaner, at six.

qa.q: What does Parveen feel watching Hrithik?
qa.a: Parveen feels some envy at how fast he is rising, but mostly worry about his shaking hands.

qa.q: Why was Parveen's sentence to Hrithik well chosen?
qa.a: It supported his goal while showing care for his health, so he could accept a break without feeling judged.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel when he asks about the walk?
qa.a: Hrithik may feel a little relieved, quietly accepting that he needs a break.

grounding: Shows a colleague watching a peer sacrifice sleep and health for promotion, offering concern without judging the goal.

passage:
Senior associate's note, for my own reflection.
Aadhya is on track for promotion faster than any of us. Honestly, I felt a pang of envy when the partners praised her again on Monday.
But I've watched the cost. She sends emails at 3 a.m. She skipped her best friend's engagement for a client deck. On Wednesday she looked grey and was holding her head during the review. She laughed it off: "Sleep is for after promotion."
I noticed I wanted to say, "Is it even worth it?" I didn't. That's her decision, and it would have sounded like judgment.
What I did next: I asked her to lunch outside the office, just the two of us. I said, "I'm not questioning your goals. I've just noticed you look worn out, and I'm worried. Would it help if I took the Friday client call?" She was quiet, then said yes.
Harish

qa.q: Whose engagement did Aadhya skip?
qa.a: Her best friend's engagement.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Harish have about Aadhya?
qa.a: Harish felt a pang of envy at her fast promotion track, but also real worry after seeing how worn out she looked.

qa.q: Why was Harish's approach at lunch a wise way to help?
qa.a: Harish showed genuine concern without questioning her goals, and offered a practical break by taking the Friday call.

qa.q: How might Aadhya have felt when Harish offered to take the call?
qa.a: She may have been surprised and relieved, since her quiet pause before saying yes suggests she needed the break but hadn't asked.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a peer sacrificing sleep and friendships for promotion, setting aside envy and offering a break out of concern.
